title: How to Choose a Facebook Ads Agency
summary: Choose a Facebook ads agency with a practical interview checklist. Compare creative, reporting, total fees and ownership before agreeing to a first-month plan.
body_markdown:
## How should you compare agency quotes?


Compare the same responsibilities, output definitions and budget period. Separate media, management, production, setup and third-party charges. Then write down the work left with your team. Our[Facebook agency pricing guide and copyable worksheet](https://knowlify.com/articles/facebook-ad-agency-pricing) give you a place to collect those answers and calculate first-month versus ongoing cost.


One proposal might include new concepts and revisions while another expects you to supply finished ads. One may have a spend-linked minimum while another has a fixed fee within capacity limits. Resolve those differences before choosing on price. If you already have a media buyer, price a separate creative partner as well as a replacement full-service team.


Buy the quantity your team can approve, launch and evaluate. A[creative subscription](https://knowlify.com/creative-as-a-service) can provide recurring production, but define what counts as an accepted ad and how revisions count. If approved work sits unlaunched, adding more assets alone does not address the queue.


## What should the first-month plan and contract include?


Agree on the sequence of work and the conditions for launch. The plan should state what you supply, what the agency delivers, who approves it and when the next decision happens. Use our[video ad approval workflow](https://knowlify.com/articles/video-ad-approval-workflow) to assign copy, product-claim and spend approvals.


Before signing, record:


1. **Inputs:** account access, approved claims, brand assets and product information.
2. **Deliverables:** concepts, finished files, formats, revisions and delivery milestones.
3. **Launch controls:** budget authority, tracking checks and the person who approves ads.
4. **Review:** reporting access, review cadence and how findings inform the next batch.
5. **Exit:** notice period, remaining fees, rights, asset handover and access removal.


Ask for unresolved assumptions to appear beside the delivery date. A plan that requires product footage or legal approval should name that dependency. If there is a guarantee, read its eligibility rules, measurement period and remedy in the written agreement.


## How do you check fit beyond the sales presentation?


Ask to see how the proposed team would handle an ordinary working decision. A portfolio shows finished work; a process example can reveal whether the agency understands your constraints and communicates clearly when something is unresolved.


Use a specific scenario from your business. For example, you may have accurate product footage but limited review capacity, or an established campaign account with nobody consistently requesting new creative. Ask the agency to explain the first decision it would make and the input it needs from you. Evaluate the reasoning rather than expecting a complete free campaign strategy.


If a reference conversation is available with that client's permission, focus on operational fit. Ask what the client had to supply, how feedback was consolidated and what happened when the original plan changed. Do not ask the reference to disclose private account data or treat its results as a forecast for your own campaign.


Compare the reference's working conditions with yours. An agency may work well with a large internal marketing team that supplies approved briefs, while your business needs much more direction. The question is whether the proposed scope accounts for the difference. Ask the agency to name the additional work rather than assuming it will happen inside the same fee.


## What should a launch-readiness review actually inspect?


Review the connection between the approved offer, creative, destination and campaign responsibilities. The purpose is to catch an unresolved dependency before it becomes a live campaign problem. Agree the actual technical checks with the campaign owner rather than treating this editorial checklist as a complete implementation specification.


For each planned ad, identify its approved file, intended destination, current offer and final approver. Confirm that the product or service shown can be purchased or requested under those conditions. If a price, feature or delivery promise changed during production, send the affected asset back for the necessary review.


Next, confirm authority. Who can authorize the launch? Who can change the media budget? Who handles an urgent commercial change such as a product becoming unavailable? A shared understanding of those decisions matters whether the same agency produces the creative and runs campaigns or two teams share the work.


End the review with a short list of ready items and unresolved items. Give each unresolved item an owner and the next action. Avoid calling the whole campaign ready merely because the videos have been delivered. Equally, do not allow a minor unrelated preference to obscure a specific launch decision that the responsible owner can make.


## How do you compare the first month with the proposal?


Create an engagement review around the promised work. Check whether the agency received the agreed inputs, delivered the expected outputs and explained changes to the plan. Separate a client dependency from a supplier delivery problem so the discussion can resolve the actual issue.


Consider an illustrative engagement promising concept development, finished ads and campaign management. If the ads were approved but never launched, determine who owned launch and why it remained open. If the client changed the offer after editing, record how the change affected the plan. If the campaign ran but the evidence is still limited, evaluate the available information without inventing a performance verdict.


Review the work your team retained. Did briefing and review take the effort you expected? Were product questions raised early enough for the right person to answer? Did reports lead to a clear decision about what happens next? Those observations help you decide whether to refine the working process or change the scope.


A useful review concludes with a specific next assignment and an owner. “Continue the demonstration concept with a clearer offer explanation” is more actionable than “make stronger ads.” Record what supports the decision and what remains a hypothesis.


## When should you choose creative only instead of a combined agency?


Choose creative-only support when your current buyer can own the campaign decisions and provide usable feedback to production. Compare a combined engagement when that ownership is missing or when you want one team responsible for making and managing the Meta ads. The decision should follow the work to be transferred, not the assumption that a larger scope is always better.

Put the responsibilities, private service price and separate media budget in the agreement. Keep your evaluation focused on whether that arrangement supplies the capability your team needs and makes the next decision easier to take.

## FAQ


### What should I look for in a Facebook ads agency?


Look for relevant work, an accountable delivery team, a clear creative process and reporting tied to your business objective. Require a written scope and total fees. The interview table above helps you compare the evidence behind each answer instead of relying on the presentation or a headline result.


### Is creative production included in Facebook ads management?


Check the proposal: Knowlify offers creative production and campaign management together through its end-to-end Facebook ads service, and also offers creative-only work. For any agency, record concepts, scripts, finished ads, revisions and campaign responsibilities in the agreement. Name an owner for any work retained by your team.


### How do I know if an agency's case study is relevant?


Compare the business model, target customer, budget, objective and measurement method with your own situation. Ask what the agency changed and which costs are counted. A strong result in a different setting is useful background, but it does not establish that the same approach or outcome will transfer to your account.


### Can I keep my current media buyer and hire an ad creative agency?


Yes. Assign the creative partner a defined production scope and agree how it exchanges briefs and findings with the media buyer. Name who requests new concepts, approves claims, uploads ads and reports results. That handoff is the practical requirement; both providers do not need to be the same company.


### How many Facebook ads agencies should I compare?


Three candidates is a manageable shortlist for this process, not an industry rule. Send each the same brief and compare responsibilities, work samples, fees and proposed next steps. Add another candidate if the current shortlist does not cover the capability you need, rather than choosing a weak fit to finish the exercise.


### Should I hire an agency that guarantees results?


Evaluate the work and evidence first, then review any guarantee as a contract term. Ask what result it measures, which conditions you must meet, how disputes are handled and what remedy is available. A guarantee does not remove your need to assess fit, approve product claims or understand the delivery plan.
